analysis.one_liner: Bans offshore oil and gas drilling off south Florida and cancels existing federal leases there.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in House subcommittees when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have permanently banned offshore oil and gas leasing, exploration, and drilling in the federal waters of the Gulf of Mexico off south Florida, and would have canceled the 73 federal leases already sold there. Leaseholders would have been compensated, with payments capped by law and Florida required to pay nothing. It was referred to two House committees and two subcommittees and never moved again before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Florida's coastal communities, tourism businesses, commercial and recreational fishermen, and residents whose beaches, reefs, seagrasses, and fisheries would be protected from drilling spills and infrastructure. The bill's text cites coral reefs, mangroves, live-bottom communities, and endangered species in the area it would close.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Florida coastal communities, tourists, and fishermen

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Interior Department from holding lease sales or permitting any exploration, production, or drilling in the Gulf area south of 26°N and east of 86°W, making the existing year-by-year drilling moratorium permanent for that area [S2][S3].
Cancels all 73 federal leases sold in that area in 1984 and 1985, removing the threat of drilling on tracts that are already under industry control [S3].

Declares in law that drilling in this area would cause serious harm to the marine, coastal, and human environment that cannot be acceptably mitigated, given the area's coral reefs, mangroves, seagrasses, and endangered species [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through compensation owed to oil and gas companies whose valid leases are canceled, capped at the formula in the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act; part of the compensation could be paid by forgiving rents and royalties those companies owe on other federal leases, which would reduce federal revenue. Oil and gas leaseholders lose the drilling rights they paid for.

drawbacks.text: C canceling already-sold leases means taxpayers compensate companies for extinguished property rights; the bill caps the payout but does not eliminate the cost, and allows part of it to be paid by forgiving royalty obligations on other leases, reducing federal revenue [S3].
Removing 73 tracts from potential production forgoes domestic oil and gas supply from the Eastern Gulf, a cost drilling supporters would weigh against the environmental protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is permanent and targeted at an area the bill text describes as ecologically unique, while the cost is a one-time, legally capped compensation to leaseholders. The main design weakness is the option to settle claims by forgiving royalties on other leases, which quietly shifts part of the price onto future federal revenue. On balance the trade favors the public, but the bill never got far enough for these terms to be tested or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and then two subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Harry Johnston of Florida introduced the bill on June 21, 1994, joined by one Republican cosponsor, Rep. Porter Goss of Florida [S1][S3][S4].
It was referred the same day to both the Natural Resources Committee and the Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee, a joint referral that split jurisdiction over offshore drilling bills [S5].
Within a week it was sent to subcommittees in both committees, and the Interior Department was asked for its views, but no hearing, markup, or floor action followed [S5].
No further action appears in the record for the rest of the 103rd Congress, which ended January 3, 1995, so the bill died in committee [S5].

The underlying protection it sought continued through other means: the record in the bill itself notes that Congress had renewed an annual moratorium on leasing and drilling in the area every year since 1988, and President Bush had announced a 10-year moratorium for south Florida in 1990, so drilling remained barred even without this bill [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas leaseholders, who kept their 73 leases because Congress never canceled them, and the existing system of temporary annual moratoria remained in place instead of a permanent ban.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas leaseholders who kept their leases

for.name: Rep. Harry Johnston
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban drilling and cancel the south Florida leases.

for.name: Rep. Porter Goss
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after receiving the referral; the bill's subcommittee assignment was its last move in that committee.

against.name: House Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Oceanography, Gulf of Mexico, and the Outer Continental Shelf Subcommittee and took no further action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan in sponsorship, a Florida Democrat and a Florida Republican, but it drew only one cosponsor total and no votes were ever taken, so no party split shows up in the record.

industries.note: The bill would cancel 73 leases these companies bought in 1984 and 1985, though they would receive capped compensation, possibly by forgiving what they owe on other federal leases. Their interest in drilling the tracts ran against protecting the reefs, fisheries, and beaches nearby.

A permanent drilling ban would protect the beaches, coral reefs, and fish stocks that Florida's tourism and fishing economies depend on; their interest runs with the coastal residents the bill aims to shield.
